title: Front loop and back loop working
subtitle: Working into one loop only changes the fabric texture and creates ridges
excerpt: Every stitch top presents two loops: a front loop and a back loop. Working through both is the standard. Working into the front loop only (FLO) or back loop only (BLO) creates horizontal ridges, folds, and textured effects.
sourceNotes: Pauline Turner, How to Crochet — single-loop working as a texture tool. Standard British crochet teaching texts.

glossaryTerms.definition: The loop of the stitch top that faces you when the work is held in the normal crocheting position. Abbreviated FLO when a pattern directs you to work into it alone.

The loop of the stitch top that faces away from you when the work is held in the normal crocheting position. Abbreviated BLO when a pattern directs you to work into it alone. The unused loop left behind creates a horizontal ridge on the fabric.

heroPrompt: Two small swatches of double crochet in cream DK cotton side by side on a pale surface — the left swatch shows standard two-loop working (smooth), the right shows BLO working with clear horizontal ridges running across each row.

content.text: A normal crochet stitch enters through both loops of the stitch top. Working into the

only (BLO) leaves the unused loop free on the surface of the fabric — and that unused loop forms a horizontal ridge. BLO working is the standard way to make the ribbed cuffs and waistbands used on hats, jumpers, and socks.
How to identify the two loops

Hold the work flat with the right side facing up. Look at the top of the row below the hook. Each stitch forms a small V. The leg of the V nearest you is the front loop; the leg furthest from you is the back loop. Tilt the work toward you if you cannot see the separation clearly.

Work every stitch into the back loop only. The front loops sit unworked on the fabric face as a continuous horizontal line, row after row. The result looks like knit-style ribbing — stretchier than normal double crochet and with clear horizontal grooves.
BLO double crochet fabric has noticeably more horizontal stretch than standard double crochet. For hat brims and boot cuffs worked sideways, BLO creates the elastic quality that holds the item on.
A fold or ridge on the right side of the fabric — the unused back loops show as a raised line.
Joining a second layer to the same row later — the free back loops provide a neat attach point.
Basketweave effects when alternated with BLO rows.

Half treble stitches have a third loop: a horizontal bar sitting behind the back loop. Some patterns direct you to work into this third loop for an even more pronounced ridge. The technique is common in Tunisian crochet hybrids and structured amigurumi patterns.
